A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ARC-JSD research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support matching content across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original attribution benchmarks, mechanistic analyses, answer-judging results and attention-masking experiments using Qwen2 and Gemma2 models.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, divergence-metric experiments and a HotpotQA hallucination-gating study.

M1.justification: The core sentence-ablation/JSD ranking and Logit Lens localization remain unchanged. However, v3 Section 7 introduces semantic-gain-dependent gating of the top-five located attention heads and MLP layers, extending the procedure from attribution analysis to actively modifying RAG responses.

E1.justification: English TyDi QA, HotpotQA and MuSiQue remain the datasets. v3 adds a downstream evaluation of hallucination mitigation while preserving factual answer quality on HotpotQA, extending the evaluated application beyond attribution and answer-agreement checking.

E2.justification: v1 Table 2 benchmarks ARC-JSD against Contextcite alone. v3 Figures 2(a), 5 and 6 additionally evaluate ALTI-Logit and MIRAGE. Its metric-comparison experiments also evaluate KL, TV, MMD and Wasserstein alternatives against JSD.

E3.justification: The original dataset sizes, development-set sampling and four model backbones remain. v3 replaces measured seconds per sample with theoretical FLOPs for efficiency evaluation, adds a 32-call Contextcite configuration and sentence aggregation for token-level baselines, and introduces a 200-case HotpotQA study with base, targeted-gating and random-gating conditions evaluated using hallucination rate and factual F1.

E4.justification: The original top-10 versus random attention-masking analysis and case studies are retained. v3 adds divergence-replacement ablations across the three datasets and a targeted-versus-random gating experiment testing whether located components can reduce hallucinations while preserving factual information.

E5.justification: Table 3 retains the same significance annotations, and Table 5 retains the same uncertainty reporting for attention masking. Neither version specifies repeated-run or seed counts. The added experiments introduce no new confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: v3 adds baseline and divergence-comparison results. New Table 4 reports hallucination rates of 13.4% for base RAG and 8.2% for targeted gating, with factual F1 of 76.1 and 75.9. Some retained attribution scores are revised: Gemma2-9B on MuSiQue changes from 78.2% in v1 Table 2 to approximately 68% in v3 Figures 2(a) and 4. The measured-runtime results are removed.

T1.justification: The central attribution, semantic-gain and consensus-ranking mathematics is retained. v3 adds approximate FLOPs formulas in Table 1 and supporting mathematical analysis in Appendix J, including computational complexities and a counterexample deriving equal TV distances for perturbations with different greedy-decoding outcomes.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes efficient attribution relative to surrogate modelling and mechanistic localization. v3 broadens its superiority claims to additional baseline classes and makes controlling RAG behavior and mitigating hallucinations an explicit primary contribution, whereas v1 identifies steering interventions as unexplored.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands the rationale for JSD over alternative distances and interprets uniformly small JSD scores as absent contextual dependence, proposing a low-evidence flag. It expands the interpretation of semantic-gain agreement and replaces the untested-intervention limitation with untested generalization to tasks such as membership inference, while retaining the neuron-resolution limitation.

D1.justification: v3 adds code-repository access information, explicitly mentions key-value caching, clarifies top-1 sentence evaluation and baseline token-to-sentence aggregation, and supplies gating parameters. The H100 hardware, NLTK sentence preprocessing and prompt templates remain unchanged. The caching mention establishes additional disclosure, not a demonstrated implementation change.

R1.justification: v3 adds Learning to Attribute with Attention, AttriBoT, the ALTI-Logit paper and two language-model scaling references. Related work expands its contributive-attribution discussion and distinguishes AttriBoT's efficiency focus, while retaining the existing corroborative/contributive and NIAH positioning.

P1.justification: The overall section sequence and much of the existing exposition remain. v3 revises introductory and concluding prose, condenses the Transformer background and semantic-gain derivations, reorganizes the case-study discussion and adds a Discussion section. Front matter changes from an under-review preprint to a NeurIPS workshop designation.

P2.justification: v3 combines the two framework diagrams into Figure 1 and combines a compute–accuracy plot with the existing mechanistic heatmap in Figure 2. The accuracy table and runtime chart are replaced by scatter plots and a FLOPs table. New gating and metric-comparison displays appear, while the attention-masking table moves into the main text and existing case-study figures are reordered.

improvement.justification: Broader comparisons address v1's narrow baseline validation, and gating investigates a previously acknowledged limitation. However, v3 removes measured-runtime evidence while broadening efficiency claims. The new metric experiments do not specify their kernel/Sinkhorn settings, and Table 4 leaves the sigmoid-versus-fixed-0.7 gating implementation ambiguous. These substantive benefits and reporting weaknesses prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
